title: The Fayyum to Sura: the Arabic Torah, the Calendar, and the Gaon Who Would Not Sign
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Fayyum and the Two Languages

stops.name: Dilaz, Fayyum: the birth
stops.date_confidence: contested: 882 or 892. The 892 date was exclusively cited before 1921; 882 rests on a Cairo Genizah list of his writings compiled by his sons. 882 is adopted here because every source gives his age at death in 942 as sixty, which 892 contradicts. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: In a village of the Fayyum, in the green depression west of the Nile where an ancient canal turns desert into wheat, a son is born to Joseph. They call him Sa'id, which his Hebrew signature makes Saadia, and the district gives him the name he carries to Iraq and never loses: al-Fayyumi, the man from the Fayyum. Egypt in these years is an Abbasid province governed from Fustat, and its Jews read the Torah in Hebrew and argue in Arabic. Two reckonings of the year of this birth survive, and they stand ten years apart.
suggested_refs: The Genizah list of Saadia's writings compiled by his sons, dated 1113, basis of the 882 birth year

stops.name: Fayyum: the schooling of a boy in two languages
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No teacher, school, or year of his Egyptian education is named in any source consulted; the date is a placement within his boyhood.
stops.campa: The boy is set to the Hebrew Bible and the rabbinic law, and at the same time to the Arabic in which every clerk, physician, and theologian of the caliphate does business. In the Fayyum the Muslim schoolmen argue the unity of God and the justice of God from reason alone, and their questions carry across the street. He learns young that a proof is a thing a man can build, and that the Torah can be defended in the language of those who dispute it. Not one of his teachers is named in anything that survives.
suggested_refs: The Mu'tazilite kalam of the Egyptian schools, reconstructed as the background of his later theology

stops.name: Fustat: the first dictionary of Hebrew
stops.date_confidence: derived, not attested. The source gives an age, 'at the age of 20', not a year: c. 902 on an 882 birth, c. 912 on a 892 birth. Location within Egypt is conventional; the canonical Fustat pin is used.
stops.campa: At about twenty he writes his first book: the Agron, a dictionary of Hebrew arranged for poets, the words gathered by their beginnings and again by their endings so that a man composing in Hebrew can find his rhyme. Nobody has done this for the language before. The Hebrew of the Bible has been recited, chanted, and expounded for a thousand years; he takes it apart into a list. He is a lexicographer before he is a philosopher or a judge, and he stays one. Whatever he later defends, he defends by first fixing what the words are able to mean.
suggested_refs: The Agron, the earliest Hebrew dictionary, later expanded into the Kutub al-Lughah

stops.name: Fustat: against the followers of Anan ben David
stops.date_confidence: derived, not attested. The source gives 'at the age of 23', not a year: c. 905 on an 882 birth, c. 915 on a 892 birth, which is also the year given for his emigration to Palestine. The later opponent Abu al-Surri ben Zuta belongs to the Babylonian years, not here.
stops.campa: At about twenty-three he writes against the followers of Anan ben David, who hold that scripture alone binds and that the oral law of the rabbis is an invention. It is his first polemic and the opening of a campaign that runs forty years. The Karaites read the verses he reads and arrive at a different Sabbath, a different calendar, a different law of forbidden marriage. Both sides are pious and both sides can cite. What is being fought over is custody of the text, and he has already decided that custody belongs to whoever can parse the Hebrew.
suggested_refs: The Ananite communities of Egypt, first target of a forty-year polemic

stops.name: Tiberias: the school of Abu Kathir
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of emigration; month and day unknown. The specific house or academy of Abu Kathir is not identified in any source consulted.
stops.campa: He comes to Tiberias on the western shore of the lake, where the men who fixed the vowels and the accents of the Hebrew Bible keep their craft, and studies under Abu Kathir Yahya al-Katib. Tiberias is the workshop of the Masoretes. Every point set beneath a letter is a decision about how the text is read aloud, and therefore about what it says. He arrives knowing the words and leaves knowing the apparatus: the grammar and the pointing on which his Arabic Bible will later stand, learned from the men who made it.
suggested_refs: The Tiberian Masoretic school, whose pointing underlies every printed Hebrew Bible

stops.name: Jaffa: the father's grave
stops.date_confidence: no year attested. The source says only that his father was compelled to leave Egypt and died in Jaffa. The date here places the stop within his Palestinian years, after the arrival at Tiberias, for sequence only, and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: His father Joseph is compelled to leave Egypt and dies at Jaffa on the Palestinian coast. The notice is one sentence long. It gives no year, it does not say what compelled the departure, and it does not say whether father and son travelled together or whether the son learned of the death by letter. The family that produced him goes dark after this: a name, a coast, a grave nobody has found. Egypt is behind him now, and he will not see it again in his life, though his writings will go back there and be buried in a storeroom.
suggested_refs: The medieval Jewish community of Jaffa, port of the Palestinian coast

stops.name: Mosul: the prayer written on the road
stops.date_confidence: c. 920/921, from Malter. The itinerary Baghdad to Arbela to Mosul to Aleppo is named in the Genizah fragment; the pin is the modern city of Mosul, one waypoint of that route.
stops.campa: He is on the road out of Babylonia, by Arbela and Mosul toward Aleppo, and he writes a prayer in the manner of the patriarchs: that the Lord who took him out of his city lead him where he means to go and bring him home in peace. He is in involuntary exile from Egypt, without a post and without a patron, moving between the two centres of Jewish learning and belonging to neither. The scrap survives because a storeroom in Fustat kept everything with the name of God on it for a thousand years.
stops.quote: Now Thy servant has set his face to go into the land of Canaan and the land of [Babylonia], for he heard that... And now, O Lord, that Thou hast taken me out of my city, mayest Thou lead me to my desire, and bring me back in peace to the house of my father. Turn me not away empty from before Thee, for in the shadow of Thy mercy I take refuge.
stops.quote_source: Cairo Genizah fragment, Schechter, Saadyana, pp. 133-135; English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), pp. 61-62
suggested_refs: Schechter's Saadyana (1903), the Genizah fragments of Saadia's own letters and prayers
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), pp. 61-62

stops.name: Aleppo: the news of the two days
stops.date_confidence: attested for the place and the episode; month unknown. The source says he learned of the decree at Aleppo, on his way from the East, that is travelling westward; it does not say he composed his treatise there.
stops.campa: At Aleppo, coming from the east, he learns what Aaron ben Meir has proclaimed out of Palestine: a change in the reckoning that sets Passover and the festivals two days earlier than the Babylonians keep them. Two days is a schism. If the two great communities eat leaven on different afternoons and fast on different days, they are no longer one people under one law. He is nobody in particular, an Egyptian scholar with no office and no academy behind him, and he begins at once to write against the head of the Palestinian gaonate.
suggested_refs: Aaron ben Meir's calendar proclamation, traditionally made from the Mount of Olives

stops.name: Baghdad: the academies close ranks
stops.date_confidence: attested to the fall of 921; day unknown. Canonical Baghdad academy pin inherited from the Benjamin de Tudela file.
stops.campa: In Baghdad the exilarch David ben Zakkai and Mar Kohen-Zedek of Pumbedita make peace between themselves, a rivalry laid down so that the calendar can be defended with one voice. David writes to Ben Meir urging him not to make a schism; when the letters fail, the ban follows, and it is the exilarch's ban, not the Egyptian's. Saadia supplies the arithmetic and the argument. The Babylonian reckoning holds. A year earlier he was an Egyptian on the road without a post; the exilarch's house now sends for him by name.
suggested_refs: The 921 concord between the exilarch and Pumbedita, prelude to the excommunication of Ben Meir

stops.name: Baghdad: the letter to the pupils in Egypt
stops.date_confidence: Malter dates the letters to the winter of 922, January to March, written somewhere in Babylonia. The exact town is not attested; Baghdad is used as the map anchor.
stops.campa: From somewhere in Babylonia he writes to his old pupils in Egypt and counts the silence: six and a half years without a word from them. He had even written to console them on the death of the old man, and no answer came. In another letter of the same winter he tells them they have probably thought he was still in Palestine. He is the coming man of Babylonian Jewry. He is also a husband and father living apart from his household, and he cannot be sure his own students could say which country he is standing in.
stops.quote: As I have been desolate ever since I left my wife and children, so I have grieved over my separation from you. May it be the will of the Almighty that I see you again in health and happiness. It is now six and a half years that no word from you has reached me. I even wrote to you condoling with you over the death of the venerable old man, blessed be his memory, but I saw no answer.
stops.quote_source: Letter to his former pupils in Egypt, c. 922, Cairo Genizah fragment (Schechter, Saadyana, pp. 24ff.); English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), pp. 55-56
suggested_refs: Malter's Postscript, p. 425, where the often-misquoted line about Palestine actually stands
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), pp. 55-56 and p. 425

stops.name: Baghdad: the Book of Festivals
stops.date_confidence: 922 attested for the work; month and day unknown. Written at the exilarch's request, which places it in Babylonia rather than at Aleppo. Canonical exilarch pin inherited from the Benjamin de Tudela file.
stops.campa: At the exilarch's request he writes the Book of Festivals, the case for the Babylonian calendar set out whole. The dispute turns on rules of postponement and on the length of the molad, the reckoned moment of the new moon, and it is settled not by revelation but by calculation carried out in the open and checked by anyone who can count. After this the fixing of the Jewish year belongs to Babylonia. The Palestinian gaonate keeps its dignity and loses the calendar, and no later authority reopens the question.
suggested_refs: Sefer ha-Mo'adim, the treatise that settled the Jewish calendar in Babylonia's favour

segments.name: Sura, the Academy Raised From the Ground

stops.name: Pumbedita: the other academy
stops.date_confidence: context stop, not a documented visit. Pumbedita's site is conventionally associated with the vicinity of modern Fallujah; coordinates approximate. Its gaon in this period is Kohen-Zedek.
stops.campa: On the Euphrates near the present Fallujah stands Pumbedita, the rival academy, richer in students than Sura and jealous of its precedence. Kohen-Zedek is its gaon in these years. Between the two schools and the exilarch's court at Baghdad the whole government of Babylonian Jewry is divided: the academies teach, judge, and answer the questions sent from Spain to Persia, and the exilarch, who traces his line to David, holds the office the caliphate recognizes and taxes. Saadia is about to be handed one of the three.
suggested_refs: The twin-academy structure of Sura and Pumbedita under the Baghdad exilarchate

stops.name: Sura at Mata Mehasya: the weaver's years
stops.date_confidence: 926 attested for the arrival at Sura. The alluf title is conventionally dated 922, but no source consulted gives it a year. Sura sat east of the Euphrates at 31 deg 53 min N, 44 deg 27 min E; a widely repeated pin west of the river is wrong.
stops.campa: He settles for good in Lower Mesopotamia, joins the academy of Sura at Mata Mehasya east of the Euphrates, and is given the title alluf. Sura is old and failing. Its endowments have thinned, its students have gone up the river to Pumbedita, and for two years the office of gaon is filled by a weaver whose name the chronicles do not trouble to keep. The school that Rav founded seven centuries earlier is a few rooms, a library, and a reputation running on memory. Saadia arrives into that, and stays.
suggested_refs: The Sura academy at Mata Mehasya, founded by Rav c. 225 and functioning until 1033

stops.name: Sura: the Book of Distinction
stops.date_confidence: 926 attested for the composition; month and day unknown. Place of composition inferred from his residence at Sura in that year.
stops.campa: He writes the Book of Distinction, the largest of his works against the Karaites, in the year he settles at Sura. The method is the one he never abandons. Take the opponent's proof text, establish the grammar, show what the Hebrew can and cannot be made to say, then show that the written law is unusable without the oral law that carries it. Scripture alone does not tell a man how to slaughter an animal or at what moment the Sabbath begins. He is arguing for an institution, and he argues as a grammarian.
suggested_refs: Sefer ha-Tamyiz, his principal anti-Karaite work

stops.name: Sura: made Gaon
stops.date_confidence: 928 attested for the appointment; month and day unknown. The sources call the choice unconventional or a contested rise; none of them says he was the first non-Babylonian to hold the office, and that superlative is avoided here.
stops.campa: David ben Zakkai raises him to the gaonate of Sura. It is a markedly unconventional choice. The office has gone by custom to the Babylonian scholarly families, and this man is an Egyptian immigrant with no dynasty behind him and a known habit of writing exactly what he thinks. The exilarch is warned about him. He appoints him anyway, wanting the one scholar in Iraq capable of putting Sura back on its feet, and gets him, together with everything else that comes with a man who does not sign what he does not believe.
suggested_refs: The gaonate of Sura, revived under an appointment from outside the Babylonian dynasties

stops.name: Sura: the Bible turned into Arabic
stops.date_confidence: no composition dates for individual books of the Tafsir are given in any source consulted; the work is treated as a body produced across the Babylonian years and placed here for sequence.
stops.campa: He translates the Hebrew Bible into Arabic and writes it out in Hebrew letters: the Torah first, then Isaiah, Psalms, Job, Proverbs and more, with commentary running beside the text. The Jews of the caliphate speak Arabic and think in it; he gives them their own scripture in that language, rendered for sense rather than word by word, with the limbs and passions ascribed to God turned into figures a philosopher can defend. It is the version Maimonides grows up on in Egypt two and a half centuries later.
suggested_refs: The Tafsir, the Judeo-Arabic Bible, still read in Yemenite synagogues a millennium later

stops.name: Sura: the order of prayer written down
stops.date_confidence: undated. No source consulted gives a year for the Siddur; the date places it within the first gaonate.
stops.campa: He compiles the order of prayer: the liturgy of a whole year gathered into one book, with the rubrics and instructions written in Arabic, so that the man holding it knows not only what to say but when to stand, when to bow, and what may be left out. He sets his own poems into it, among them the Azharot, the six hundred and thirteen commandments versified for the feast of the giving of the law. Custom had been carried in the memory of congregations. He writes it down, and a written custom can travel.
suggested_refs: Kitab Jami al-Salawat wal-Tasabih, among the earliest systematically compiled prayer books

stops.name: Sura: the answers going out
stops.date_confidence: undated. The responsa and the named Karaite opponents are attested; the exact date and location of individual exchanges are not specified in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The gaon's daily labour is the responsum. Questions arrive at Sura from Qayrawan, from Fustat, from Spain and from Persia: a disputed inheritance, a doubtful divorce, a word in the Talmud nobody can construe. The answers go back signed, and they are copied and cited as law. Against the Karaites he keeps writing, at Salmon ben Yeruham, at Ibn Saqawayhi, at Abu al-Surri ben Zuta. The academy that was a few rooms and a weaver is again the address to which the whole diaspora writes when it does not know what to do.
suggested_refs: The geonic responsa, the legal correspondence of Sura and Pumbedita with the diaspora
sources: Jewish Virtual Library and Encyclopaedia Judaica summaries, reached through secondary citation

stops.name: Sura: the seventy hard words
stops.date_confidence: undated. No year is attested for the Kutub al-Lughah or for the list of rare words; the date places them within the gaonate.
stops.campa: He keeps at the language all his life. The Agron of his twenties grows into the Kutub al-Lughah, the books of the language, in which Hebrew is given a grammar of its own instead of rules borrowed from elsewhere. He also draws up a short list of some seventy rare words of the Bible, words that occur once or twice and that nobody can construe, and explains them from the Hebrew of the Mishnah. That little list is copied and reprinted for centuries. He is doing for Hebrew what the grammarians of Basra and Kufa did for Arabic.
suggested_refs: Tafsir al-Sab'ina Lafza, the list of seventy rare biblical words, reprinted for centuries

segments.name: The Document He Would Not Sign

stops.name: Baghdad: the exilarch's message
stops.date_confidence: the inheritance case itself is undated in the sources. Its outcome is fixed at the beginning of 933, and the litigation reached a caliph who died in 932, so c. 932 is the earliest defensible onset. A date of 928 in circulation is the year of his appointment, not of the case.
stops.campa: An inheritance case comes before the exilarch's court, and David ben Zakkai decides it in a manner that serves David ben Zakkai. For the ruling to stand it needs the signature of both geonim beneath his own. Mar Kohen-Zedek of Pumbedita signs it. The document goes down to Sura and comes back unsigned. The exilarch does not send a jurist to argue the law with the man he appointed. He sends his own son Judah with an instruction, and behind the instruction stands the office that made Saadia gaon and can unmake him.
stops.quote: Go and tell him in my name that he shall at once endorse the documents.
stops.quote_source: David ben Zakkai to his son Judah, in Nathan ha-Bavli's Report; English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), p. 110
suggested_refs: Nathan ha-Bavli's Report, the near-contemporary chronicle of the quarrel
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), p. 110

stops.name: Baghdad: the answer out of Deuteronomy
stops.date_confidence: same undated episode as the preceding stop; the sequence within it is attested by Nathan ha-Bavli, the dates are not.
stops.campa: Judah carries the exilarch's word into the presence of the gaon and gets scripture back. It is written in the Torah, Saadia tells him: you shall not respect persons in judgment. Nothing in the sentence is about David ben Zakkai and everything in it is. Four years earlier this patron made him gaon of Sura. He now declines to treat the patron as a special case, and says so by quoting the verse that forbids it, to the patron's son, in the patron's own city. Everything after comes out of that answer.
stops.quote: Tell your father that it is written in the Torah, 'Ye shall not respect persons in judgment.'
stops.quote_source: Saadia to Judah ben David ben Zakkai, quoting Deuteronomy 1:17, in Nathan ha-Bavli's Report; English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), p. 110
suggested_refs: Deuteronomy 1:17, the verse cited across the exilarch's threshold
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), p. 110

stops.name: Baghdad: sign and do not be a fool
stops.date_confidence: same undated episode; sequence attested, dates not. Nathan ha-Bavli is the sole source for the exchange and Malter the sole translation consulted.
stops.campa: The son goes back across the city and returns with a second message, which is no longer an argument or an order but a taunt: sign, and do not be a fool. It fails as the first failed. Judah leaves the gaon's presence defeated and goes home in tears, and the chronicler who writes within living memory of these men keeps the detail of the weeping. Within a year there are two bans, two exilarchs, two geonim of Sura, and a petition on the desk of a caliph. It begins with a document and a man who will not put his name on it.
stops.quote: Sign and don't be a fool!
stops.quote_source: David ben Zakkai's second message to Saadia by his son Judah, in Nathan ha-Bavli's Report; English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), p. 110
suggested_refs: Malter (1921), p. 111, where Judah goes home 'with tears running from his eyes'
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), pp. 110-111

stops.name: Sura: deprived of the gaonate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the beginning of 933; month and day unknown. A date of 930 in circulation confuses the deposition with the outbreak of mutual excommunication.
stops.campa: At the beginning of the year the exilarch deprives him of the gaonate and puts in his place Joseph ben Jacob ben Satia, a man of no weight whose one qualification is that he will sign. Five years after the appointment that pulled Sura out of the ground, Saadia walks out of it holding no office. The chair he leaves is the chair of the school of Rav, and the man now sitting in it holds it as a favour granted. The quarrel has stopped being about an inheritance and has become a question of who governs.
suggested_refs: Joseph b. Jacob b. Satia, installed at Sura in 933 and unseated four years later

stops.name: Baghdad: the second exilarch
stops.date_confidence: attested that the counter-deposition followed the deposition of early 933; the month is inference from that sequence. A date of 930 in circulation is wrong.
stops.campa: He answers in kind. If an exilarch can depose a gaon, a gaon can depose an exilarch. Saadia declares David ben Zakkai removed and proclaims David's own brother, Josiah called Hasan, exilarch in his place. Now there are two exilarchs and two heads of Sura, each with a following, each pronouncing the ban on the other, and the Jews of Iraq must decide in which court their marriage contracts and their deeds are good. Both parties then take the quarrel where such quarrels end under the caliphate.
suggested_refs: Josiah Hasan, brother of David ben Zakkai, raised as rival exilarch in 933

stops.name: Baghdad: the caliph decides
stops.date_confidence: 933 attested for the ruling; month and day unknown. That the case was heard by al-Muqtadir, who died in 932, and then by his successor al-Qahir independently pushes the start of the litigation back into 932.
stops.campa: The rival parties petition the Abbasid court, the caliph al-Muqtadir and, after his death, his successor al-Qahir, and money moves as it always moves in such petitions. The judgment goes to David ben Zakkai. He keeps the exilarchate. His brother Josiah is sentenced to banishment, and Saadia is left out of office in a city where he has just been ruled against by the government, having made an enemy of the man that same government has confirmed. Twenty years of polemic against the Karaites had cost him nothing but ink. This costs him the academy.
suggested_refs: The Abbasid court under al-Muqtadir and al-Qahir, arbiter of the exilarchate

stops.name: Nishapur: the road east
stops.date_confidence: banishment attested to 933; no date is given for his death in Khorasan, and no town within the province is named. Nishapur is a conventional anchor for the historic region, not an attested site.
stops.campa: Josiah called Hasan, exilarch for a matter of months, is carried off to Khorasan by order of the caliph, into the far northeast of the Abbasid world, and dies there. The sources say nothing further: not the town, not the year, not the manner of it. Of everyone the quarrel touched, he is the one it removed entirely. Saadia keeps his life, his library, and his pen, and the man he raised up against the exilarch disappears at the eastern edge of the map with no grave anyone records.
suggested_refs: Khorasan, easternmost reach of a quarrel that began over a signature at Sura

stops.name: Baghdad: the sea of doubt
stops.date_confidence: 933 attested for the completion of the work, from Wikipedia; the Stanford Encyclopedia gives no date for it. No source consulted names his residence during the deposition, so the Baghdad pin is a map convenience and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: Out of office and with nothing to administer, he writes the book that makes him a philosopher. The Book of Beliefs and Opinions argues in Arabic, in the order and the vocabulary of the Muslim theologians, that the world was made out of nothing, that its Maker is one, and that revelation and reason cannot finally contradict each other because both issue from the same source. It is the first systematic theology any Jew has written. He gives his own reason for it in the preface: men are drowning and nobody is diving after them.
stops.quote: My heart grieved for mankind, and my soul was moved on account of our own people Israel, as I saw in our times many of those who adhere to their faith entertain impure beliefs and unclear ideas, while those who deny the faith boast of their unbelief and triumphantly deride the men of truth, albeit they are themselves in error. I saw men sunk, as it were, in a sea of doubt and overwhelmed by the waves of confusion, and there was no diver to bring them up from the depths and no swimmer to come to their rescue. But as God has granted unto me some knowledge by which I can be useful to them, and endowed me with some ability which I might employ for their benefit, I felt that to help them was my duty and guiding them aright a moral obligation upon me.
stops.quote_source: Kitab al-Amanat wal-I'tiqadat (Book of Beliefs and Opinions), Introduction; English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), p. 200
suggested_refs: Kitab al-Amanat wal-I'tiqadat, the first systematic work of Jewish philosophical theology
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), p. 200

stops.name: Baghdad: the humors and the colors
stops.date_confidence: the passage belongs to the Book of Beliefs and Opinions and carries no separate date; placed with that work. Residence unattested, as above.
stops.campa: Inside the same book he turns to the senses, and to what a mixture does. Red with yellow rouses the choleric humor and the soul shows energy and vigor; yellow with black brings the phlegm forward and the soul is cast down; green with yellow stirs the black humor and produces timidity and sadness. The argument underneath is about proportion. Nothing in the created order is good raw and unmixed, and the religious life consists in compounding rightly what would be poison taken by itself.
stops.quote: Red combined with yellow stimulates the choleric humor and its properties; the soul then manifests energy and vigor. Yellow mixed with black makes the phlegmatic humor predominate, producing in the soul a state of dejection. A combination of black, red, yellow, and white sets into action the sanguine humor; the soul then manifests a will to power and dominion. Finally, a combination of green and yellow stirs up the black humor (melancholia), producing in the soul timidity and sadness.
stops.quote_source: Kitab al-Amanat wal-I'tiqadat, on the psychological effects of color combinations; English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), p. 259, note 542a
suggested_refs: Saadia's doctrine of sensory harmony as the analogue of moral equilibrium
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), p. 259 n. 542a

stops.name: Baghdad: the Open Book
stops.date_confidence: undated. Sefer ha-Galui is attested as written during the David ben Zakkai controversy, but no source consulted gives it a year or a place.
stops.campa: He writes in Hebrew as well, in the biblical manner with the accents and vowels supplied, an apology for his own conduct in the quarrel, and calls it the Open Book. Against it comes the exilarchal letter of excommunication, a document his modern biographer can compare for baseness only with the diatribe of Sarjadah, the son-in-law who is keeping the fire alive. Saadia's own answer to the whole affair is a sentence about providence. No generation is left without a teacher, and he does not say who the teacher is.
stops.quote: God does not leave His nation at any period without a scholar whom He inspires and enlightens, so that he in turn may so instruct and teach her, that thereby her condition shall be bettered.
stops.quote_source: Sefer ha-Galui (The Open Book), quoted as the epigraph of Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), front matter
suggested_refs: The exilarchal Letter of Excommunication, Harkavy, Zikron, V, p. 232, not read directly here; Malter's characterization stands at p. 112
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), front matter and p. 112

stops.name: Baghdad: the Book of Creation and the two hundred questions
stops.date_confidence: undated on both counts. The Stanford Encyclopedia lists the Sefer Yetzirah commentary among his works but gives it no date and no place; the c. 931 date in older reference literature is not attested in the sources cited here. The Hiwi al-Balkhi refutation is likewise undated and unplaced.
stops.campa: He takes up the Book of Creation, the small dark ancient text on the ten numbers and the twenty-two letters by which the world is said to be made, and writes an Arabic commentary on it, reading its cosmology as physics rather than as magic. He also answers Hiwi al-Balkhi, whose questions against the Bible had been circulating among Jewish students and, it was said, taught to children. The objections are already in circulation, so he answers them in circulation, one point at a time, rather than moving to have them suppressed.
suggested_refs: Tafsir Kitab al-Mabadi, the Arabic commentary on the Sefer Yetzirah
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica summary of the polemical corpus, reached through secondary citation

segments.name: The Reconciliation and the Last Chair

stops.name: Baghdad: the community goes to Bishr ben Aaron
stops.date_confidence: c. 936-937, inferred from the reconciliation date of 27 February 937. The episode is attested by Nathan ha-Bavli; its own date is not.
stops.campa: David ben Zakkai has manhandled a litigant whose case went the other way, and Baghdad has watched him do it. The community goes to Bishr ben Aaron, a man of standing with access to the exilarch, and tells him to move, since the strife is fed by nobody so much as his own son-in-law Sarjadah. Four years of rival courts, mutual bans, and a petition at the caliph's door end in a private house, where merchants and scholars agree that one respected old man should go and say the obvious.
stops.quote: Rise to action, for it is your duty, and we shall assist you in the effort to put an end to this strife, which is fomented only by your son-in-law Sarjadah.
stops.quote_source: Baghdad Jewish community representatives to Bishr b. Aaron, in Nathan ha-Bavli's Report; English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), p. 121
suggested_refs: Nathan ha-Bavli's account of the Baghdad notables who brokered the peace
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), p. 121

stops.name: Baghdad: the reconciliation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 27 February 937.
stops.campa: Bishr goes to the exilarch and speaks to him as nobody else will: see what you have done, how long will you keep up this quarrel without fearing God's punishment. On the twenty-seventh of February the two men are reconciled in public. Neither has yielded on the inheritance case that began it and neither is asked to. What has changed is that the Jews of Iraq have spent four years watching their two heads excommunicate each other before a Muslim court, and both men can now count what that has cost.
stops.quote: See what you have done! How long will you keep up this quarrel without fearing God's punishment? Fear your God and desist from strife, for you know how grave are its consequences. It is time now that you try to improve your conduct toward Saadia, that you make peace with him, and abandon whatever grudge you have against him.
stops.quote_source: Bishr b. Aaron to Exilarch David ben Zakkai, in Nathan ha-Bavli's Report; English translation in Henry Malter, Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works (1921), pp. 122-123
suggested_refs: The reconciliation of 27 February 937, ending four years of rival courts
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921), pp. 122-123

stops.name: Sura: restored to the chair
stops.date_confidence: restoration attested as following the reconciliation; no separate date is given for it in any source consulted.
stops.campa: He goes back down to Mata Mehasya and to the chair, and holds it for the rest of his life. Joseph ben Jacob ben Satia leaves it without a struggle and vanishes from the record. Five years remain. He governs the academy, answers the questions that come in from the diaspora, keeps writing, and supports Judah, the son of David ben Zakkai, as the next exilarch: which is to say he underwrites the succession of the house that deposed him. Nothing suggests either man ever reopened the document.
suggested_refs: The second gaonate of Sura, 937 to 942

stops.name: Sura: the enemy's grandson
stops.date_confidence: David ben Zakkai's death in 940 and Judah's death seven months later are attested; the exact months are not given. The boy's name is not recorded.
stops.campa: David ben Zakkai dies. His son Judah, who once carried his father's threats to Sura and went home weeping, succeeds him and dies seven months later, leaving a boy of twelve. Saadia takes the child into his own house, educates him, and keeps him there. The man who deposed him is dead; the son who was sent against him is dead; the last of that line is being raised at the table of the gaon they tried to break. He continues it, the chronicler says, until his own death, which is two years off.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Exilarch', on the twelve-year-old grandson taken into Saadia's household

stops.name: Sura: the black gall
stops.date_confidence: 16 May 942 attested for the death, and age sixty, which fits the 882 birth. The place is contradicted: Wikipedia gives Sura, the Stanford Encyclopedia gives Baghdad. The two are not reconciled here.
stops.campa: He dies at Sura, sixty years old, of what his son Dosa called black gall: the melancholy humor, the same one he had described years before as the mixture that makes the soul timid and sad. Sixty years from a village in the Fayyum, and he leaves behind him a Bible in Arabic, a calendar settled for good, and an academy he pulled twice out of the ground. A second reference source of standing puts the death at Baghdad instead, and the two accounts do not agree.
suggested_refs: Abraham ibn Daud, Sefer ha-Qabbalah, reporting his son Dosa on the cause of death
sources: Abraham ibn Daud, 'Sefer ha-Qabbalah', via Wikipedia

stops.name: Baghdad: the other tradition of the death
stops.date_confidence: the year is agreed; the place is not. The Stanford Encyclopedia states he died in Baghdad in 942, directly against Wikipedia's Sura. Flagged as an unresolved contradiction between the two principal reference sources.
stops.campa: A reference tradition of good standing gives Baghdad, not Sura, as the place where he died. The two accounts cannot both be right and no source consulted decides between them. It is at least plausible that by the end the academy's business and the gaon's own household were not in the same town, since the exilarch's court, the caliph's court, and the money were all in Baghdad, and Sura lay ninety miles down the Euphrates. Where the body lay in that May of 942, nobody now knows.
suggested_refs: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saadya', which places the death at Baghdad

stops.name: Safed: the burial nobody witnessed
stops.date_confidence: no date and no evidence. The only support is an uncited encyclopedia infobox field whose internal link is dead; the date here is a placement after the death and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: An encyclopedia box names the old Jewish cemetery of Safed in the Galilee as his burial place. There is no citation behind the line and the link it offers goes nowhere. No tomb, no marker, no pilgrimage, no local tradition of a grave of Saadia is described in anything consulted, and nothing of the kind is recorded at Sura either. The man who spent his life insisting that a claim name its source has no attested grave anywhere, in Iraq or in the Galilee, and the attribution is late.
suggested_refs: The Old Jewish Cemetery of Safed, named without citation as his burial place
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saadia Gaon' (uncited infobox field, dead internal link)
Wikipedia, 'Sura Academy' (no tomb or remains recorded)

stops.name: Lunel: turned into Hebrew and answered back
stops.date_confidence: the Ibn Tibbon translation is traditionally dated to the late twelfth century; 1186 is conventional and the Lunel pin is the Tibbonid family seat, not an attested place of composition. The quoted English of Ibn Ezra is the editor's looser rendering; the primary text is his commentary on Genesis 2:11.
stops.campa: In Provence the Tibbonids turn the Judeo-Arabic philosophers into Hebrew for readers who no longer have Arabic, and Judah ibn Tibbon renders the Book of Beliefs and Opinions as Emunot ve-Deot. In that dress it enters the philosophical tradition of Latin Europe, and Jews who cannot read a word of Saadia's own language argue with him for centuries. In the same west Abraham ibn Ezra reads his identifications of the biblical rivers and lands and refuses them, on the ground that the man had no tradition for it, only a dream.
stops.quote: He doesn't have an oral tradition... perhaps he has a vision in a dream, while he has already erred with respect to certain places...; therefore, we will not rely on his dreams.
stops.quote_source: Abraham ibn Ezra, Commentary on Genesis 2:11, in a widely circulated English rendering; the published translation of Strickman and Silver (Menorah, 1988) reads 'The fact of the matter is that he had no tradition concerning these things ... Perhaps these things were revealed to him in a dream. He definitely erred in a number of them ... So we will not rely on his dreams.'
suggested_refs: Ibn Ezra's commentary on Genesis 2:11, verified in the Hebrew via Sefaria
sources: Abraham ibn Ezra, Commentary on Genesis 2:11 (Piotrkow 1907-1911 ed., via Sefaria)
Strickman and Silver, 'Ibn Ezra's Commentary on the Pentateuch' (1988)

stops.name: Yemen: the copyists in the highlands
stops.date_confidence: continuous manuscript transmission across many centuries; the date is a placeholder inside that span, not an event.
stops.campa: For centuries the Jews of Yemen keep copying the Tafsir by hand. Elsewhere the Arabic Bible falls out of use as the communities that needed it change language or disappear. In the highlands it stays in the codices beside the Hebrew and the Aramaic, read aloud in the synagogue verse by verse, week by week, in a country the caliphate stopped governing long ago. The book he made for the Arabic-speaking Jews of an empire outlives the empire, preserved by the community furthest from the road.
suggested_refs: Yemenite manuscript codices carrying the Tafsir beside the Hebrew and the Targum

stops.name: Fustat: the storeroom gives him back
stops.date_confidence: the Ben Ezra Genizah was cleared from the 1890s; Schechter published the Saadia material as Saadyana in 1903. The date marks the recovery period, not a single event.
stops.campa: The storeroom of the Ben Ezra synagogue at Fustat, where worn-out paper bearing the name of God was thrown rather than burned, holds fragments of his Bible translation, his responsa, his grammar, and the letters he wrote from Babylonia to pupils in Egypt who had not answered him in six and a half years. Scholars empty the room at the end of the nineteenth century and print what they find. His complaint about their silence comes back out of Egyptian rubbish a thousand years after he wrote it.
suggested_refs: The Ben Ezra Synagogue genizah at Fustat, source of Schechter's Saadyana
sources: Henry Malter, 'Saadia Gaon: His Life and Works' (1921)
S. D. Goitein and later Genizah scholarship

stops.name: Jerusalem: the Yemenite editor
stops.date_confidence: 1970 for the first appearance of Qafih's Judeo-Arabic edition with facing Hebrew. The 2011 imprint cited in some bibliographies is a posthumous reprint: Qafih died in 2000.
stops.campa: Yosef Qafih, born in Sana'a and trained in the tradition that kept Saadia's Arabic alive when nobody else wanted it, edits him in Jerusalem: the Tafsir, and the Book of Beliefs and Opinions in its Judeo-Arabic original with a Hebrew translation facing it. Of that original only fragments had been known to survive into the twentieth century. He works from the manuscripts his own community carried. The people who kept the text by hand for a thousand years supply the man who sets it in type.
suggested_refs: Qafih's edition of Sefer ha-Nivhar ba-Emunot uva-De'ot, Judeo-Arabic with facing Hebrew, 1970

stops.name: Tel Aviv: a street and no face
stops.date_confidence: the street exists; no date of naming is attested. The claim that other Israeli cities also carry his name is not in the cited source and is not made here.
stops.campa: Modern Israel commemorates him with a street, Se'adya Ga'on, at its junction with the street of the Hasmoneans. There is no portrait. No contemporary or medieval likeness of him is attested anywhere: no icon, no coin, no describing hand, nothing that records whether he was tall or how he wore his beard. What remains of him is text: printed editions, and a name lettered on a street sign at a corner in a city that did not exist in his lifetime. The boy who made the first list of Hebrew words ends as an entry on a list.
suggested_refs: Sderot Sa'adya Ga'on, Tel Aviv, at the junction with HaHashmona'im
